title: The business case in agile: value and the MVP
blurb: Explain how the business case practice works in agile: a focus on value, the most valuable features first, the MVP and the fixed minimum viability of benefits.
question: A chief product owner ranks every user story by the value it adds to the project's objective and schedules the highest first. Which business case guidance is she applying, and why does it matter?

teach.h: The business case practice, agile style
teach.body: The purpose of the business case practice does not change in agile: it gives mechanisms to judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable, to support decisions on continued investment. What agile adds is a strong focus on value: every piece of work should contribute to meaningful outcomes, so the most valuable work is done first and checked with real users early.

In agile, the focus on value means each effort should directly contribute to meaningful outcomes for users and stakeholders. Prioritizing value keeps attention on solutions that solve real problems, raise user satisfaction and support business goals. A practical way to do it is to assign a value to each user story and prioritize stories by their value to the project's objective.

teach.caption: Deliver from the top down. Low-value stories are the first to drop if time runs short.

teach.h: Two 'minimums' that are easy to confuse
The MVP in the business case
teach.body: The MVP (minimum viable product) is a basic version built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback. In PRINCE2 Agile it helps assess product viability by testing core features with minimal investment; in highly innovative work it means validating key assumptions quickly. If an MVP is used, the project canvas must identify it, so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be delivered later than expected.

teach.h: Fix and flex for the seven aspects (Table 3.1 rows)
head: Aspect
PRINCE2 Agile default
rows: Fixed: zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Fixed: zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Fixed for Must haves; flexed for Should and Could haves
Fixed for minimum viability; flexed above it
Fixed for minimum criteria; flexed above them
teach.caption: Quality and risk rows are not shown here. Agile flexes what is delivered and protects time and cost.

items.label: Photos and ratings, if time allows

teach.caption: Frequent releases are planned so benefits can start before the project ends.

teach.body: Kestrel Bay Ferries wants online vehicle bookings to cut call-centre demand. Chief product owner Priya Raman gives each user story a value score against that objective. Booking and paying come first as the MVP, released to one route to test whether drivers use it. The project canvas sets a minimum benefit, a fixed drop in phone bookings, and treats anything above it as flexible. When a supplier delay threatens the stage, the team drops low-value stories rather than extending the date.

teach.text: The MVP is a product idea (a basic version for early feedback); minimum viability is a benefits idea (the floor that is fixed in Table 3.1). Also, valuing work does not mean doing the cheapest or easiest stories first: it means doing what contributes most to the objective first.

items: Business case purpose (6.1): desirable, viable and achievable, now and throughout.
Agile adds a focus on value: every effort should contribute to meaningful outcomes.
Assign value to each user story and deliver the most valuable first.
The MVP tests core features with minimal investment; the canvas must identify it.
Benefits are fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it (Table 3.1).
Time and cost are fixed; Should have and Could have scope flexes to protect them.

summary: You can now explain how the business case practice focuses on value in an agile project and why the most valuable features come first. You can also tell the MVP apart from the fixed minimum viability of benefits.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what is meant by the 'focus on value' in the business case practice?
options: Every effort should add directly to meaningful outcomes
The cheapest user stories should be delivered first
Value is measured once, at the end of the project
The project canvas should list every requested feature
A.why: Book 6.3.1: the focus on value means every effort contributes directly to meaningful outcomes for users and stakeholders.

whyNot.1: Value is about contribution to the objective, not about which stories cost least.
whyNot.2: Value guides prioritization throughout, and benefits can be confirmed during the project.
whyNot.3: The canvas summarizes scope as epics or main features; value focus is about prioritizing, not listing everything.

A.q: What is a practical way of applying the focus on value in an agile project?
options: Ask the project board to approve each user story
Assign a value to each user story and prioritize by it
Deliver user stories in the order they were written
Leave value decisions to the delivery team's tester
A.why: Assigning value to each user story and prioritizing by value against the objective puts the focus on value into practice (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: The board directs the project; it does not approve individual stories.
whyNot.2: Order of writing says nothing about value to the objective.
whyNot.3: Testers check work against acceptance criteria; prioritizing by value sits with product ownership.

A.q: Under PRINCE2 Agile defaults, how are benefits treated?
options: Flexed fully, with no minimum set
Zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Fixed for minimum viability, flexed above
Fixed at the full forecast in the canvas
A.why: Table 3.1: benefits are fixed for minimum viability and flexed above minimum viability.

whyNot.0: There is a fixed floor: minimum viability.
whyNot.1: Zero tolerance on all levels of plan applies to time and cost.
whyNot.3: Only the minimum is fixed; benefits above it can flex.

B.q: Why must the project canvas identify the MVP, if one is used?
options: So the team can skip the Definition of Done for it
So the board can approve each MVP story in turn
So the MVP replaces the benefits management approach
So an exception can be raised if it is forecast late
B.why: Table 6.1: the MVP, if used, must be identified so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be delivered later than expected.

whyNot.0: The Definition of Done still applies to MVP work.
whyNot.1: The board does not approve individual stories; it works by exception.
whyNot.2: The benefits management approach stays; it plans frequent releases for early benefits.

B.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what does the MVP help the business case practice to assess?
options: Product viability, by testing core features cheaply
Team capability, by mapping skills, levels and gaps
Risk exposure, by tracking total risk across iterations
Supplier cost, by comparing competing contract bids
B.why: Book 6.3.1: the MVP helps assess product viability by allowing testing of core product features with minimal investment.

whyNot.1: Mapping skills and gaps is the team skill matrix (organization practice).
whyNot.2: Tracking total risk levels is the cumulative risk burn-down chart (risk practice).
whyNot.3: Comparing bids belongs to procurement and the commercial management approach.

B.q:
Which two statements about value in the agile business case are correct?
1. The most valuable user stories should normally be delivered first.
2. Benefits have zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
3. An MVP is a complete product with every Must have and Should have.
4. Benefits above minimum viability can be flexed.
options: 1 and 4
1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: Value focus puts the most valuable stories first (6.3.1), and benefits are flexed above minimum viability (Table 3.1).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: zero tolerance on all levels of plan applies to time and cost.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: benefits have a fixed minimum with flex above, and an MVP is not a complete product.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is wrong: an MVP is a basic version for early feedback.

C.q: A stage is forecast to overrun. The minimum benefit level can still be met if two low-value Could have stories are dropped. What is the PRINCE2 Agile default response, and why?
options: Extend the stage, as benefits are fixed in full
Increase the budget, as scope is fixed in agile
Drop the Could haves, as time is fixed and they flex
Cut a Must have, as benefits flex above the minimum
C.why: Time is fixed with zero tolerance, scope flexes for Should and Could haves, and benefits are fixed only at minimum viability, which is still met (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance, and benefits are fixed only at the minimum, not in full.
whyNot.1: Cost has zero tolerance; scope is fixed only for Must haves.
whyNot.3: Must haves are fixed scope; the Could haves are the right items to flex.

C.q: A board member says the MVP and 'minimum viability' are the same thing. Which response is correct?
options: They match: both are fixed with zero tolerance
They differ: the MVP is a time tolerance, minimum viability is cost
They match: both are set out in the risk register
They differ: one is a basic product, the other a benefits floor
C.why: The MVP is a basic product version for early feedback (6.3.1); minimum viability is the level of benefits that is fixed, with flex above it (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Zero tolerance applies to time and cost; neither concept is defined that way.
whyNot.1: Neither is a time or cost tolerance.
whyNot.2: The MVP is identified in the project canvas; minimum viability is a benefits default in fix and flex.

C.q: Which principle does the agile focus on value and the MVP MOST directly support?
options: Manage by stages
Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Learn from experience
C.why: In agile, ensuring continued business justification (5.2.1.1) is supported by the focus on value, the MVP, the project canvas and frequent releases, which keep the project worthwhile throughout.

whyNot.0: Manage by stages concerns planning and authorizing one stage at a time.
whyNot.2: That principle concerns the project's roles and stakeholders.
whyNot.3: Learning from experience is supported by retrospectives and feedback loops, but value and the MVP serve justification.

reteach.title: Spend the first pound where it earns the most
reteach.question: If you could only fit five items in your suitcase, would you pack the most useful ones or the first ones you found?

blocks.body: With a fixed-size case (fixed time and cost), you pack the most useful items first. If space runs out, the nice-to-haves stay at home. Agile business cases work the same way: rank stories by value, deliver the top ones first, and let the low-value ones go if time is short. The trip must still be worth taking: that is the fixed minimum of benefits.

blocks.text: MVP = smallest useful product. Minimum viability = smallest acceptable benefit. Different things, both called 'minimum'.

explain.body: The business case practice judges whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable, to support decisions on continued investment (6.1).

test.q: The business case practice judges whether the project is desirable, viable and:
options: affordable
achievable
agile
approved

whyNot.0: Affordability is part of viability, but the third term is achievable.
whyNot.2: Being agile is a way of working, not one of the three tests.
whyNot.3: Approval is a board decision informed by the business case.

explain.body: Assign value to each user story and prioritize by value to the objective, so the work that matters most is done first.

test.q: A team has time for three more stories. Which should it choose, applying the focus on value?
options: The three newest stories
The three smallest stories
The three stories the PM likes
The three highest-value stories
test.why: The focus on value means prioritizing the stories that contribute most to the objective (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Age of a story is not a measure of value.
whyNot.2: Priorities come from value to the objective, set with product ownership.

explain.body: A basic version with minimal cost and time, to get early feedback and test core features. If used, the project canvas must identify it so a late forecast can trigger an exception.

test.q: What is the purpose of an MVP?
options: To deliver the full scope in one release
To get early feedback from a basic version
To fix the benefits at their full level
To replace the project canvas
test.why: An MVP is a basic version built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: An MVP is deliberately not a complete product.
whyNot.2: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability, not in full, and that is not the MVP's purpose.
whyNot.3: The project canvas stays and should identify the MVP.

explain.body: Table 3.1 fixes benefits for minimum viability and flexes them above it. Time and cost are fixed with zero tolerance.

test.q: Which aspect is fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it?
options: The benefits
The scope
The cost
The timescale
test.why: Benefits: fixed for minimum viability, flexed above minimum viability (Table 3.1).

whyNot.1: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves.
whyNot.2: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
whyNot.3: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
